⁂ _Seeing how much Monsieur the Vicomte d'A....... occupies the public’s attention, Monsieur the Vicomte Demosthenes said yesterday:—Perhaps they will leave me in peace now._

⁂ _A lady said to an Ultra who was criticizing Monsieur Pasquier’s speech as a continuation of Decazes’s system:—Yes, but he has very monarchist calves._

—If it begins like this, I ask no more of you; everything is going well, said Finot. Run and take this to them, he said to the apprentice. The paper is a little patched together, but it is our best issue, he said, turning toward the group of writers who were already looking at Lucien with a kind of slyness.

—That fellow has wit, said Blondet.

—His article is good, said Claude Vignon.

—To table! cried Matifat.

The duke gave his arm to Florine, Coralie took Lucien’s, and the dancer had Blondet on one side and the German minister on the other.

—I do not understand why you are attacking Madame de Bargeton and Baron Châtelet, who, they say, has been appointed prefect of the Charente and master of petitions.

—Madame de Bargeton threw Lucien out like a scoundrel, said Lousteau.

—Such a handsome young man! exclaimed the minister.

The supper, served on new silverware, on Sèvres porcelain, and on damask linen, breathed substantial magnificence. Chevet had prepared the supper; the wines had been chosen by the most famous merchant on the Quai Saint-Bernard, a friend of Camusot, Matifat, and Cardot. Lucien, who for the first time saw Parisian luxury in operation, thus went from surprise to surprise, and concealed his astonishment like the man of wit, heart, and style that he was, in Blondet’s words.

As they crossed the drawing room, Coralie had whispered in Florine’s ear:—Get Camusot so thoroughly drunk for me that he will be obliged to remain asleep at your place.

—So you have _made_ your journalist? Florine replied.

—No, my dear, I love him! Coralie retorted, with an admirable little movement of her shoulders.

These words had resounded in Lucien’s ear, carried there by the fifth deadly sin. Coralie was admirably well dressed, and her attire skillfully brought her particular beauties into relief; for every woman has perfections of her own. Her dress, like Florine’s, had the merit of being made of a delightful new fabric called _silk muslin_, whose first offering belonged for a few days to Camusot, one of the Parisian providences of the Lyon factories, in his capacity as head of the Golden Cocoon. Thus love and attire, that cosmetic and that perfume of woman, heightened the attractions of the happy Coralie. An anticipated pleasure, one that will not escape us, exerts immense seductions upon young men. Perhaps certainty is, in their eyes, the whole attraction of houses of ill repute; perhaps it is the secret of long fidelities? Pure, sincere love, first love in short, joined to one of those fanciful fits of passion that excite these poor creatures, and also the admiration caused by Lucien’s great beauty, gave Coralie the wit of the heart.

—I would love you ugly and sick! she said in Lucien’s ear as she sat down at table.

What words for a poet! Camusot disappeared, and Lucien no longer saw him when he looked at Coralie. Could a man who was all enjoyment and all sensation, bored by the monotony of the provinces, drawn by the abysses of Paris, weary of poverty, tormented by his forced continence, tired of his monastic life in the Rue de Cluny and of his fruitless labors, withdraw from this brilliant feast? Lucien had one foot in Coralie’s bed and the other in the birdlime of the Newspaper, toward which he had run so hard without being able to catch it. After so many watches mounted in vain in the Rue du Sentier, he found the Newspaper seated at table, drinking chilled wine, merry and good-natured. He had just been avenged for all his sufferings by an article that, the very next day, was to pierce two hearts into which he had wished, but in vain, to pour the rage and pain with which he himself had been drenched. Looking at Lousteau, he said to himself:—There is a friend! never suspecting that Lousteau already feared him as a dangerous rival. Lucien had made the mistake of displaying all his wit: a dull article would have served him admirably. Blondet counterbalanced the envy devouring Lousteau by telling Finot that one had to capitulate to talent when it was of such strength. This judgment dictated Lousteau’s conduct: he resolved to remain Lucien’s friend and to come to an understanding with Finot in order to exploit so dangerous a newcomer by keeping him in need. It was a course quickly decided upon and understood in its full extent between the two men through two phrases spoken from ear to ear.

—He has talent.

—He will be demanding.

—Oh!

—Good!

—I never sup without fear with French journalists, said the German diplomat with calm and dignified good nature, looking at Blondet, whom he had seen at the Comtesse de Montcornet’s. There is a saying of Blücher’s that you have been charged with making come true.

—What saying? said Nathan.

—When Blücher arrived on the heights of Montmartre with Sacken in 1814—forgive me, gentlemen, for taking you back to that fatal day for you—Sacken, who was a brute, said: So we are going to burn Paris!—Take great care not to; France will die only of _that_! Blücher replied, pointing to the great canker they saw spread out at their feet, ardent and smoky, in the valley of the Seine. I bless God that there are no newspapers in my country, the minister resumed after a pause. I have not yet recovered from the terror caused me by that little fellow with the paper hat who, at ten years of age, possesses the reason of an old diplomat. And so, this evening, it seems to me that I am supping with lions and panthers who do me the honor of sheathing their claws in velvet.

—It is clear, said Blondet, that we can tell Europe, and prove to it, that Your Excellency vomited up a serpent this evening, that you nearly inoculated Mademoiselle Tullia, the prettiest of our dancers, with it, and, on that basis, make comments about Eve, the Bible, and the first and last sin. But do not be alarmed: you are our guest.
